items.body: Laibach release “MUSICK : ENCORE” on Mute on 20 November 2026, on vinyl, CD and digitally. The companion piece to this year’s “MUSICK” combines unreleased material from the original album sessions with new remixes from SILVERWINGKILLER, Richard X, The Lincolnshire Poacher and PUNCHBAG. MUSICK : ENCORE by Laibach The album leads with two new tracks. “This Is The End” features Slovenian singer Kaja Skrbinšek, while a new version of “Love Machine,” featuring Balkan vocalist Senidah, is remixed by Mute labelmates PUNCHBAG. Senidah also appears on a second version of “Love Machine,” remixed by UK producer The Lincolnshire Poacher. Electropop producer Richard X co-produced several album tracks and remixes “Resistencia,” which also features MRFY member Gregor Strasbergar. Ghanaian artist Wiyaala, whom Laibach first saw performing in an underground club in Ljubljana, appears on two new versions of “Musick”: the Unsick version and a remix by the band’s own guitarist, Vitja Balžalorsky, credited here as Balžalorsky. Long-time Laibach vocalist Marina Mårtensson features on new track “#US,” which SILVERWINGKILLER also remixes, and on “Faith No More” alongside Joker Out guitarist Bojan Cvjetićanin. Koala Voice frontwoman Manca Trampuš features on new track “Modern Talking.” The vinyl edition carries a 10-track selection; the CD and digital editions expand to 13 tracks with the additional remixes. The digital and CD tracklist: “This Is The End” (feat. Kaja Skrbinšek), “Yom Kippur,” “#US” (feat. Marina Mårtensson), “Tales From The Crypt,” “Faith No More” (feat. Marina Mårtensson and Bojan Cvjetićanin), “Musick” (feat. Wiyaala) (Unsick version), “Resistencia” (feat. Gregor Strasbergar) (Richard X remix), “Love Machine” (feat. Senidah) (PUNCHBAG remix), “#US” (feat. Marina Mårtensson) (SILVERWINGKILLER remix), “Modern Talking” (feat. Manca Trampuš), “Allgorhythm” (feat. Wiyaala) (Algorithm remix, assisted by iTurk), “Love Machine” (feat. Senidah) (The Lincolnshire Poacher remix) and “Musick” (feat. Wiyaala) (Balžalorsky remix). “Yom Kippur” previously appeared as a standalone single featuring the Palestinian Children’s Choir, released in October 2025. On the new material, Laibach state: “Perhaps these are the final moments when creating music purely for enjoyment still carries broader significance – before alien, generative intelligence outplays and outperforms us all. So, we seized the moment.” Laibach tour dates for 2026 Laibach continue the “MUSICK” tour through the autumn with UK and European dates, including a show at London’s Islington Assembly Hall on 29 September: 25 September – Ljubljana (SI), Kino Šiška 26 September – Ljubljana (SI), Kino Šiška 29 September – London (UK), Islington Assembly Hall 30 September – Manchester (UK), Ritz 1 October – Southampton (UK), 1865 2 October – Canterbury (UK), The Gulbenkian 4 October – Gent (BE), Democrazy 6 October – Bochum (DE), Zeche 7 October – Nijmegen (NL), Doornroosje 8 October – Hamburg (DE), Große Freiheit 36 9 October – Oslo (NO), Rockefeller Music Hall 11 October – Copenhagen (DK), Bremen Teater 13 October – Berlin (DE), Huxleys Neue Welt 14 October – Dresden (DE), Reithalle 15 October – Brno (CZ), Fleda 16 October – Zagreb (HR), Boogaloo Further European dates are scheduled into 2027, including Milan, Bologna, Lausanne, Paris, Nancy, Winterthur, Vienna, Budapest, Bucharest, Thessaloniki, Athens and Benidorm. About Laibach Laibach formed in 1980 in the mining town of Trbovlje, Slovenia, evolving out of Dejan Knez’s earlier band Salto Mortale. The group co-founded the Neue Slowenische Kunst art collective with the IRWIN and Scipion Nasice Sisters Theatre groups in 1984. Their name was officially banned in Yugoslavia in 1983 after a controversial television appearance, a ban lifted in 1985 following the release of their second album, “Nova Akropola,” on Cherry Red Records. Laibach signed to Mute Records for their 1987 album “Opus Dei,” which paired subversive cover versions of Opus’s “Live Is Life” and Queen’s “One Vision” with original material, and went on to release “Let It Be” (1988), “Kapital” (1992) and “NATO” (1994), the latter reworking “The Final Countdown” and other pop and military anthems. The band’s best-known lineup – Milan Fras on vocals, Dejan Knez, Ervin Markošek and Ivan “Jani” Novak – carried Laibach through the 1990s and 2000s, spanning albums including “Jesus Christ Superstars” (1996), “WAT” (2003) and “Volk” (2006). Knez left the group in 2003. More recent studio work includes “Spectre” (2014), “Also Sprach Zarathustra” (2017), “The Sound of Music” (2018), “Wir sind das Volk (ein Musical aus Deutschland)” (2022) and the symphonic work “Alamut” (2022), alongside “Sketches from the Red District” and the “Love Is Still Alive” EP, both from 2023. Milan Fras remains lead vocalist, joined by Ivan “Jani” Novak, longtime vocalist and guitarist Marina Mårtensson and guitarist Vitja Balžalorsky. Recent singles have included covers of “Strange Fruit,” “White Christmas” and Bijelo Dugme’s “Top,” released as “Die Kanone” with Goran Bregović in 2025, plus the “Yom Kippur” single that October. Laibach unveiled “Musick” ahead of its 2026 release on Mute, the group’s most pop-leaning album to date. “MUSICK : ENCORE” extends that record with new songs and remixes, arriving 20 November 2026.
items._cn_summary: 斯洛文尼亚工业先驱 Laibach 公布续作《MUSICK : ENCKE》，延续其跨文化实验路线。这张专辑将原专辑未发行素材与多位客座艺术家及混音作品整合，包括巴尔干歌手 Senidah、加纳艺术家 Wiyaala、巴勒斯坦儿童合唱团参与的曲目，以及来自 SILVERWINGKILLER、Richard X、PUNCHBAG 等制作人的再诠释。乐队成员来自不同地域和文化背景，电子节拍与民族声乐并存，形成工业电子与世界音乐融合的丰富织体。乐队成员在声明中将这张作品置于人工智能全面取代人类创作的临界点上探讨，强调当下纯粹为愉悦而创作音乐的意义。

items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦荷兰低音提琴演奏家Arjen Gorter的职业生涯，详细回顾了他从阿姆斯特丹街头音乐启蒙、偶然接触低音提琴，到1966年与Willem Breuker合作并参与其Kollektief长达三十余年的历程。文章并非单纯评介某张专辑，而是将Gorter置于欧洲前卫爵士低音提琴演奏家的谱系中加以定位，强调其作为Breuker乐团基石的稳固节奏支撑作用，同时也指出他独立于Breuker之外的持续创作。文本梳理了Gorter早期与Gunter Hampel等德国自由爵士场景的合作线索，展现了1960年代欧洲即兴音乐网络的运作方式。全文以历史叙事为主，信息量丰富，适合对欧洲自由爵士史和低音提琴演奏传统感兴趣的读者深入阅读。

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items._cn_summary: 钢琴家兰·布莱克与歌手多米尼克·伊德合作的专辑《Roots & Byways》，核心特征在于布莱克对曲目的极端并置——将麦克斯·罗奇的政治作品与惠特尼·休斯顿的流行金曲、传统民谣与法国香颂放置在同一框架内，揭示表面无关材料之间的深层肌理与骨骼结构。布莱克不做传统意义的诠释，而是对材料进行类似核磁共振的扫描，让熟悉的旋律以全新的面貌呈现。歌手伊德的加入为布莱克的开创性钢琴语言提供了人声维度，与此前合作的珍妮·李、克里斯汀·科雷亚、萨拉·塞尔帕等歌手形成对比。伊德不像科雷亚那样根植于比莉·假日传统，也不像塞尔帕那样执着于克制，而是以逐字逐句雕琢的方式塑造歌曲，歌唱中洋溢着深切喜悦，即便面对明格斯的暗色调作品也如此。专辑的感染力正来自这种溢出框架的情感表达。

items.body: Corre [koh-ra] Correlate (verb) To have a mutual relationship or connection, in which one thing affects or depends on another… Music collective Corre fuse the natural with the synthetic and the classical with the electronic. The two styles are on opposite ends of the musical rainbow, but they can and do work effectively together, coalescing into one, their unity producing another prime example of music’s deep contrasts and contradictions. The collaboration is only seven months old (beginning in March of this year), and this gives the music a fresh appearance, shooting out electrifying lightning bolts that give the music a healthy pulse of spontaneity as well as a flexibility to rival that of a rhythmic gymnast. Soon to be released on Akira Records, Form is Corre’s debut album. The two collaborators are aiming to create a multi-media, cross-genre alliance, and the first fruits are already ripening – their recent video, created by artist Hattie Ellis, fuses naturalistic photography with a series of digital manipulations – ghosts in the system – to create a thoroughly modern and visually striking film. Opposites supposedly attract, and this blending really works. The modern and the contemporary intermingle with the accepted classical sound – the past shaping the present – sharing the space. One never outstrips the other. In music, all is one… An ambient blurring occurs when the harmonies bathe in a washed-out, slow-burning progression which, in centuries past, could have graced the sheet music in a classical recital. The textures here are a lot thicker. In ‘Response’, a piano repeats a series of soft, gorgeous chords, lights are lowered and the electronics are toned down. Muted electronics with soft edges glide around, and gentle rhythms cycle throughout the tracks. Sometimes, the electronic rhythms are absent, drifting out and away from the track, and that leaves the piano to play on in its layered atmosphere. The notes are as soft as the sea air and are always in transit, but they move slowly and thoughtfully as they go from one place to another. Stuttering, staccato-based rhythms punctuate the muted piano chords with the dash-dot-dash of morse code. Their quick-fire response is a crucial part of the music, capturing the magical thrill of spontaneity and bottling it up. Sometimes, the best things are done on impulse. www.cargocollective.com/correcreative

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: Analog Africa 厂牌发行的这张合辑聚焦贝宁传奇乐队 Orchestre Poly-Rythmo 与创作核心 Antoine Dougbé 1977 至 1982 年间的合作录音。Dougbé 被称为"魔鬼首相"，是伏都教信仰的实践者，其标志性的创作方式是以击打双腿配合 Cavacha 节奏——这一律动由鼓手 Belobi Meridjo 从火车节奏中提炼，后风靡整个中部非洲流行乐坛。音乐根基深植于 1970 年代的 Sato 和 Sakpata 放克传统，同时明显吸收了古巴 son 与刚果伦巴的影响，合成器与塑料质感的吉他音色体现了 80 年代初的录音特征。乐评通过对《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》等曲目的具体分析，展示了作品如何在循环的高帽节奏上构建层次分明的器乐对话，展现了这位短暂而高产的创作人与乐队之间独特的化学反应。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

Recorded on July 18, 1980, the album captures live versions of seven solo songs by Vega. The performance in Kansas City came just weeks before the late Suicide frontman put out his debut solo LP, and was joined by guitarist Phil Hawk for the set. The release of Live At Max's Kansas City will mark the first time that the live recording has been made available on vinyl and streaming platforms. Listen to lead track 'JUKEBOX BABY (Live At Max's... The post New Alan Vega Live Album Captures 1980 Kansas City Show Recording appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 本文介绍Alan Vega的现场专辑《Live At Max's Kansas City》，收录1980年7月18日在堪萨斯城Max's Kansas City演出的七首个人作品录音。演出由Vega与吉他手Phil Hawk合作完成，时间距离他首张个人专辑发行仅数周。这是该录音首次以黑胶和流媒体形式发行，由Sacred Bones厂牌作为Vega档案系列的一部分推出。Alan Vega作为传奇二人组Suicide的主脑，其个人现场延续了极简合成器与粗粝人声的特质，融合早期工业噪音与proto-punk的原始张力。作为见证其从乐队向个人项目过渡时期的重要现场文献，该专辑对研究纽约地下场景的演变具有参考价值。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — One of Radiohead's founding guitarists (and still member) Ed O'Brien releases his second studio album as a solo artist. I don't know any of the guest musician/collaborators but you can bet that Ed had his pick of the cr'me de la cr'me!1. "Incantations" (7:41) a single repeating acoustic guitar arpeggio provides the bed for 1:45 of Ed's folk singing. It honestly sounds like something from an early Roy Harper album. Other instruments, hand percussives and electronics, join in to move the music into territory previously traveled by the likes of DONOVAN and BJ'RK. Floating background vocals sound like Bj'rk's Inuit Choir on the Vespero tours. At 5:40 the percussionist(s) are joined by drums, electric bass, electric guitars, and keyboard atmospherics--which play out until slowly being faded out while Dave Okumu's bass and Ed's reverberating guitar notes continue to the song's end. Cool song! (13.875/15)2. "Blue Morpho" (6:18) another really cool atmospheric sonosphere created by guitars, wordless vocals, bass, synth washes, and, this time, full symphony strings. It's quite lovely--even moving: chords and multiple melody lines floating, flowing, shifting, morphing, and melding into one gorgeous textural feast. And the whole time I'm feel quite a little debt owed (or homage given) to George Martin and The Beatles. (Think of songs like "Blackbird" and "I Am the Walrus" as well as albums like Magical Mystery Tour.) Brilliant and beautiful! (9.75/10)3. "Sweet Spot" (4:10) double lines of picked acoustic guitar chords woven into one though coming from both sides of the stage starts out this beautiful, atmospheric and kind of eerie (like GRAVENHURST) music over/within which Ed sings both lead and backing vocals. I like the way the orchestra strings slowly move to the fore as Ed's lead voice sinks into the instrumental mix. Eventually, the strings (and, I'll assume, keyboard electronics) end up alone, finishing the song after everybody/everything else has left. Not as memorable as the previous songs but rewarded for the creative sound and structural tactics. (9/10)4. "Teachers" (5:18) a funky bass 'n' drum pattern is surrounded and permeated by eerie atmospherics. Ed's heavily-treated ghost-voice enters toward the end of the first minute, singing in a pleasant monotone for a minute or so but then it leaves, whereupon the bass, drums, guitars, and synths all seem to spread out into loose, adventurous swaths away from but still anchored in the main theme. The final minute sees the vocal choir sing, "open wide" before the instruments all stop or fade away, leaving only weird electronic noises to close out the song. (8.875/10)5. "Solfeggio" (2:36) guitar/electronic harpsichord chord perpetuated with sustain and arpeggiation open this before more layers of voice-originating atmospherics enter and steer the with an eerie yet unthreatening kind of melody line, repeated over and over before signing off with a final lower-register three-note sequence, all the while the glitchy electronica effects are increasingly present, even rising to a driver's position, like something from a SyFy Continuum soundtrack experience (think Au4's "Everyone Is Everyone [and Everything Is Everything]"). More genius song/sound making. (4.4375/5)6. "Thin Places" (2:19) flute, wordless voice, synthetics all woven together to create a kind of dream-like out-of-body astral travel experience. (4.4375/5)7. "Obrigado" (9:53) a very cool, almost jazz-lite rhythm track over/within which Ed & Co. deliver some pretty awesome atmospherics (as well as vocals). The reverse-delay guitar effects for Ed's guitar solo in the seventh and eighth minutes are only surpassed by the dreamy psychedelic soundscape floating and morphing beneath it (and, later, by the amazing wordless vocal tracks raging in the background--which I think one must attribute to Clare Torey-inspired Awsa Berstrom). Ed's ultra-cool voice reminds me of both George Harrison, Gadi Caplan, Donovan, and Harry Nilsson as well as, you know, Radiohead. Really a cool, amazing, and powerful song. A pleasure to listen to every single time I do. (19.5/20)Total Time 38:15It's weird how much/how often I hear core/key Radiohead sounds in Ed's music here. This leads me to feel strongly how important and integral he was/is to the Radiohead sound--to their music.A/five stars; a brilliant display of creative/innovative sound and song crafting that stands out as a masterpiece of extrapolated future music (as if Ed's projecting himself into the 22nd Century or beyond--or even another dimension). A modern musical masterpiece. Highly recommended. One of the best albums I've heard from 2026.

items.body: Review by higgins — There are debuts that sound like debuts, with that mixture of timidity and overreach so typical of someone still searching for their place, and there are debuts that arrive already carrying the astonishing confidence of people who've been playing together for half a lifetime without anyone quite noticing. Datura Lodge decidedly belongs to this second lineage. And it's no coincidence: Nicky B and W. have known each other and played together since their teens, something that comes through in every breath of this self-titled album, a chemistry that can't be improvised or bought in any studio, however good it may be.I listened to this record thanks to a promo copy the label was kind enough to send me, and I'm deeply grateful for it, because Datura Lodge is one of those works you'd rather have stumbled upon yourself, tripping over it in a record shop, and yet here we are, with the good fortune of having had it in hand ahead of time.The New Jersey duo doesn't hide its sources, nor should it. There's a melodic streak that leads straight back to Genesis, especially in those moments when the vocal reaches for the hook without giving up harmonic complexity. And there's something else too, something of our own era: that way of organizing the chaos, of metering out the tension and releasing it at exactly the right moment, which inevitably brings to mind a more restrained Steven Wilson, or his band Porcupine Tree on the days it decides to smile.Tracks like "Stone" or "Can" show that technique serves emotion rather than the other way around, with an instrumental display (Adam Holzman is in there on keys, contributing a great deal) that never tips into gratuitous showmanship. But it's in the fragility of "Hole" or the almost uncomfortable honesty of "Them" where Datura Lodge reveals its true nature: an album that knows how to laugh at itself while talking about rootlessness, generational disillusionment, and the strange task of staying human amid a full digital shipwreck.Datura Lodge doesn't reinvent progressive rock, but it inhabits it with a naturalness and a joy of playing that are sorely missed in so many current releases, more concerned with orthodoxy than with life.
items._cn_summary: 新泽西二人组Datura Lodge的首张同名专辑展现了长期合作积累的默契，乐评指出其根源可追溯至Genesis式的旋律与和声追求，同时融入了Porcupine Tree时期Steven Wilson式的结构控制力。键盘手Adam Holzman在编曲中贡献颇多，技术服务于情感表达而非炫技。专辑探讨了无根感、世代幻灭与数字化废墟中保持人性的主题，部分曲目如《Hole》与《Them》展现了脆弱与坦诚的内省气质。乐评认为该作并未重塑前卫摇滚，但以自然流畅的演奏乐趣胜出，这种品质在当前过度注重正统性而忽视生命力的作品中尤为稀缺。整体属于扎实的前卫摇滚新作，在类型传统内展现了真诚的表达。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The affirmation often has a psychological value that operates at an unconscious level; it begins from the outside and ends up taking hold internally. The Yes Album was a new beginning for many reasons: the first to feature Steve Howe, the first in which the compositions of Anderson, Chris Squire, and soon Howe would acquire that classic status and the first where rock, jazz, and a distinctive balance between acoustic and electric elements would find their signature style and a home within the progressive universe.There are many classic Yes lineups, and although the subsequent era might be considered the "classic of classics," the 1971 period is already worthy of that title. Gathering at Langley Farm, they recorded a handful of songs that would become enduring favorites, not only for that lineup but for those that followed, and have been performed live ever since.I'm a fan of the Peter Banks era, but Steve Howe, while retaining that affinity for rock 'n' roll, jazz, and classical music, brought a rhythm, a groove, and a fingering style, along with a cosmic dimension, that set the band apart right from "Yours Is No Disgrace." The vocal harmonies, often bordering on a cappella, were just one of many hallmarks that emerged with this album. The band also gained a warmth and an intimacy it hadn't possessed before; tracks like "Yours Is No Disgrace" featured not only instrumental sections but also intimate moments that made for a complete experience."Clap" is the first of many acoustic tracks by Steve Howe; composed of several sections, some with a pastoral, rustic feel and others with a distinct rock-and-roll vibe, the version that made the final cut was recorded live at London's Lyceum Theatre and would forever define one of the facets of this new Yes."Starship Trooper" must be one of the first tracks that made me fall in love with the band. Jon was gradually reaching the peak of his expressive potential, conveying a genuine emotion that was reinforced by Chris Squire on bass, Bill Bruford on drums, and, son, Steve Howe on guitar (who already seemed like a full-fledged member, even though Peter Banks still appeared on the album cover!). There was a palpable sense of communion as they focused on conveying their musical vision. Tony Kaye was solid, too, though he would later be succeeded by someone with such a massive aura that it would elevate "Starship Trooper" to even greater heights. Once again, the vocal harmonies and Jon's voice stood out... and just as the emotion reached its peak, "W�rm", the third section, would kick in. Steve would start off solo, with the rest of the band gradually joining him, creating a soundscape that felt like the prelude to a space voyage and the actual liftoff. And the first of many memorable riffs with an electrifying personality.The emotional momentum didn't let up, as a powerful new surge of feeling arrived with "I've Seen All Good People", a track that is 100% Yes. The band always drew sustenance from both the technical/virtuosic side and the spiritual/emotional one; neither works without the other, and it was their combination that gave birth to their best songs and albums. The track is neatly divided into two parts: the acoustic first section, "Your Move", which carries an almost Andean feel, and the rock-driven second half, "All Good People." The two work in tandem, creating the song's magical contrast."A Venture" is an atypical and unusual track within the context of the �lbum, and a very beautiful one. It features very interesting breaks and syncopated drum and guitar work from Howe and Bruford; towards the end, Chris's bass and Tony Kaye's distinctly jazzy solo leave you wishing they would keep playing like that for even longer."Perpetual Change" is the final track, and Bill Bruford's presence is as notable as it is significant; the format, an elaborate introduction leading into a fully developed song, set a precedent for what was to come. Hints of a country feel followed by a jazz-inflected progression, along with the polyrhythms and counterpoint in the finale, exemplified the band's high level of technical proficiency. Meanwhile, the vocal interplay between Jon and Chris offered a different facet, helping to create an album that holds a unique place in history. There are many layers to consider: while the band's subsequent work was undoubtedly more complex and elaborate, and is rightly regarded as some of their best, this album possesses its own distinct value. It stands as an equally great record, not for the same reasons as the later material, but for others; after all, as we have seen, Yes is a multi-dimensional band.
items._genre: progressive rock / symphonic prog / classic rock / acoustic
items._cn_summary: 《The Yes Album》是Yes乐队1971年的转型之作，新吉他手Steve Howe的加入为乐队注入了新的活力。专辑在摇滚、爵士与古典元素之间寻找平衡，开创了乐队标志性的声学与电声交织风格。Steve Howe的吉他演奏兼具乡村田园感与摇滚律动，其创作的多段式作品如"Clap"成为经典。Jon Anderson的声乐表达在此时已逐渐达到巅峰，配合Chris Squire的低音、Bruford的鼓点以及Tony Kaye的键盘，形成层次丰富的和声与情感张力。"Starship Trooper"的第三段"Würm"以渐进式的编配营造出太空旅行般的音景，预示了乐队后续更为宏大的艺术方向。整体而言，这张专辑确立了Yes在前卫摇滚领域的美学基调。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — On his Bandcamp page's "liner notes" Tom lists his "Gear used":Fender Rhodes Mk2 (1, 2, 3, 6)Hohner Pianet C (1, 3, 6)Hohner Cembalet I (1, 3, 6)Columbia Elepian (1)Hammond L122 (1, 3, 4, 5, 6)Roland SH2000 (1, 3, 6)SeagullS12 (1, 3, 6)Gibson SG (1, 6)Gibson Les Paul Goldtop (1, 4)Jacobacci LJ612 double neck (1, 2, 3, 6)Fender JazzbassYamaha Rydeen drumkit1. "Didier Dandelion in the Year of the Great Winds" (13:24) sophisticated, more serious Canterbury Style music of the NATIONAL HEALTH sort. A lot of displaying of some mighty fine drumming beneath/within a multi-keyboard vamp. There is a lot of very immersive melodic music here. The multi-instrumentalist seems hell-bent on proving to the world his skills and talents on guitars and keyboards, too. (He is pretty good!) All in all, this is pretty good if sounding a bit like an extension of the 1970s Phil Miller-Dave Stewart-David Sinclair expressions of sophisticated Canterbury Jazz Fusion. The music of this song doesn't always propel--doesn't always feel as if it's moving forward (which was, when I think about it, one of the frequent failings/flaws of the Canterbury artist's music)--but it is an excellent rendering of that era's sound and style. And don't miss the nod to TONY BANKS/Genesis in the "Mad Man Moon" reference in the ninth and tenth minutes as well as the excellent Phil Miller guitar work--which later turns into near-ALLAN HOLDWORTH stuff!--as well as Tom's great drumming. (27.5/30)2. "Mandatory Intermission" (3:47) a piece that feels like a true nod to the most unique genius of the Jazz-Rock Fusion movement: Allan Holdsworth. Even when Tom chooses to settle back into a fuzzy electric guitar over gentle-yet-erudite J-R F band support the lead and music carries with it a kind of reverent "history" of the many stages of growth of the great jazz guitarist: from Bradbury to 'Igginbottom to Nucleus to The Soft Machine up unto the Tempest Jean-Luc Ponty era. Nice homage! (9/10)3. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 1st Movement" (5:21) a Canterbury-inspired weave of bass, drums, electric piano, and guitar that shifts in tempo and dominant (most forward) instrument/sounds between several motifs, including one that introduces a bunch of different keyboard and guitar sounds (including 12-string guitar) while allowing electric bass and drums to remain fairly consistent. I am very much reminded of ANTHONY PHILLIPS and even MIKE RUTHERFORD with a lot of the soundscapes, melodies, and thematic shifts. There's even a little Mike Oldfield in some of the nostalgic melodies and instrumental sound choices, but when Maureen Peircy's "The Northettes'" vocals enter at 4:21 I'm totally taken off guard. Part of me is offended that someone would so blatantly "lift", copy, or replicate such a sacred element of the Canterbury tradition. At the same time, I so welcome and enjoy the brief exposures to the sounds and stylings of these old guys. (9/10)4. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 2nd Movement" (5:35) more Canterbury homage and comfort food. It's as if AI were asked to write some new Dave Stewart (Egg, Khan, Hatfield & The North, National Health) music. It's just too perfect, too much like a re-animation of the old guys: even the production values feel as if I'm listening to some newly-found tapes from 1975 (probably found under the floorboards of the old seaside Wyatt cottage in Lydden [Wellington House]--or better yet--found inside a hash cache inside the walls of Daevid Allen's Bananamoon Observatory in Dei� [Majorca]). I love it while at the same time find myself squirming uncomfortably at the "authentic" feel and sound of the music. I absolutely LOVE hearing more of the peak Canterbury style sound palette--especially when it is rendered so faithfully and so lovingly as this, but more: this is just a great piece of music no matter who did it (or when it was done). (9.25/10)5. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 3rd Movement" (6:18) this one's a little different: harkening back to some of the more sophisticated, mathematical "thought experiments" that Dave Stewart might have had back in the 1970s. There is a feeling of aloneness, even reclusiveness to this piece--even with the participation of the ghosts of Mont Campbell and Clive Brooks (or Richard Sinclair and Robert Wyatt) playing bass and drums, respectively. Even the classical music-mirroring three-part construction harkens back to the work and style of Mont Campbell's EGG trio. Though this replicates some of the early Canterbury music that I am not as attached to as others, I do appreciate its faithful replication of the sound and spirit of one of my all-time favorite eras of music. (8.875/10)6. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 4th Movement" (11:50) more modern replication of the sounds and spirit of the uniquely "Canterbury" style geniuses of the 1970s composed, performed, and rendered with truly loving detail. The organ chordplay in the movement's opening minute so remind me of the genius mathematical musings of the great Dave Stewart that I almost tear up. After the 90-second intro enter piano, drums, bass, and electric guitar, gearing up into a real rip-roarer of woven tongues of flame. In the fourth minute the quartet takes a sharp turn down one of the country roads as if on a long descent from the high ground down toward the sea and its beaches and waves--where everything smooths out and soothes the soul. Here Tom chooses to introduce the lead guitar: and lo! and behold! It's Mike Oldfield (or, at least, the ghost-spirit of). I love the infusion in this piece of riffs and stylings from other realms of 1970s prog: Mike Oldfield's guitar in the sixth and seventh minutes, Tony Banks' electric piano sound and stylings, even some sound and chord play that is a nod to Jean-Luc Ponty (in the eighth minute). There is definitely genius (as well as infinite reverence) in this man's compulsion to create (and re-create) music of the artists and magical eras gone by. I find it hard to find fault with this amazing rendering. It even ends with the sound of the tolling of the church bells of some ancient gothic church as if to re-affirm the timeless and universal place that these musics have in our lives. (23/25)Total time: 45:51A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of lovingly-replicated Canterbury Style music. If you love the era, the unique sound and style of those mythical Rainbow artists, you will find yourself melting to the music on this album. Highly recommended.
items._genre: Canterbury Scene / jazz fusion / progressive rock
items._cn_summary: Tom Penaguin 的第二张专辑延续了七十年代坎特伯雷场景的精神，以多键盘与电吉他的交织复刻 Phil Miller、Dave Stewart、Allan Holdsworth 等大师的声响质感。整张专辑由一位多乐器演奏者独立完成，鼓、贝斯、键盘与吉他并行铺陈，既有 National Health 式的复杂器乐结构，也穿插对 Genesis 的致敬段落。曲目中大量使用 Fender Rhodes、Hammond L122 等复古键盘，配合双颈吉他与十二弦原声吉他，营造出浓厚的复古爵士融合氛围。评论者对作品的技术完成度给予肯定，但也指出音乐推进力不足、过于沉浸在对旧日风格的复刻中。专辑在小型独立平台发行，体量与声场偏向个人化的复古回溯，与当下前卫实验语汇的关联较为有限。

items.body: “En La Mar”, one of the best loved songs in the Ladino repertoire and one that also travels under the name “La Sirena”, strands a maiden alone in a tower above the sea, calling to the sailors going past, wanting love and wanting out. Rachel Valfer sings her in the Judeo-Spanish that Sephardic Jews took with them when Spain expelled them in 1492 and the Ottoman Empire gave them shelter. David Mac Lean‘s flamenco guitar brings Andalusia back to the song, and the players around it mark where the song went instead: Dan Cantrell on accordion, Faisal Zedan on Arabic percussion, Eliyahu Sills on upright bass and on the bansuri he has played with the group since their first album in 2009. The track comes from Entre Las Huertas, released on 28 August, the third album by the Bay Area’s Qadim Ensemble and the first given over entirely to Ladino. Most of it comes from the kantigas, the songs Sephardic women kept and handed on, so the record runs through lullabies, a wedding party number and a mother unloading about her straying husband while she rocks the baby to sleep. Valfer and Sills have run the group from Berkeley for close to twenty years, she singing in seven languages after six years studying maqam and Persian dastgah in Israel and Palestine, he moving between ney, oud and bass. For this album they went into the studio and played, cutting most of the record live before guests came in with flamenco guitar and qanun. Stream “En La Mar” HERE and take home Entre Las Huertas through THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: The Qadim Ensemble x Rachel Valfer x Eliyahu Sills – En La Mar appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由旧金山湾区的Qadim Ensemble创作，是他们第三张录音室作品，也是首张完全围绕拉迪诺语（Ladino）的专辑。拉迪诺是1492年西班牙驱逐犹太人后，塞法迪犹太人在奥斯曼帝国庇护下保留的犹太-西班牙语。专辑曲目大多源自kantigas——由塞法迪妇女世代传承的歌谣，涵盖摇篮曲、婚礼歌谣以及母亲在摇婴儿入睡时抱怨丈夫外出不归的生活场景。主唱Rachel Valfer曾在以色列和巴勒斯坦学习六年maqam和波斯dastgah，能以七种语言演唱，Eliyahu Sills则穿梭于ney、oud和贝斯之间。编曲融合弗拉门戈吉他、阿拉伯手鼓、班苏里笛、手风琴、低音贝斯和卡侬琴，将安达卢西亚的根源与塞法迪流散后的中东轨迹交织在一起。多数曲目以现场同期录音方式完成，保留了传统民谣与跨文化即兴对话的原始质感。

items.body: Don’t you know I could love you better Be your release when you’re under pressure All that you hold, we could hold together I could be, I would be if you let me Somewhere inside I Could Love You is a person pacing around a room, rehearsing the case for why somebody ought to love them back. Every argument has already been prepared: I understand you, I can carry some of this weight, I can protect you, I can give you something better. None of it changes the verdict. With this new single, Midniter takes us somewhere between genuine tenderness and the dangerous confidence of believing you know what another person needs. Nic Pugh sings it without burying himself beneath theatrical anguish. The melody keeps drawing him toward the same impossible proposition, while piano and synthesizers give the track a strange openness, almost too much room for these thoughts to wander around unchecked. You can hear why Pugh calls it a ballad, although its emotional center feels closer to fixation slowly becoming aware of itself. “I Could Love You came from an old piano tune that I never finished,” Pugh reflects. “The bookends of the song are directly from that idea, with the middle evolving into a more synthpop direction for Midniter. To me, it’s a pretty standard ballad about unrequited love – a tale as old as time that everyone can understand.” The interesting part is how quickly “I could love you” changes meaning when repeated often enough. At first it sounds generous. Later it begins carrying frustration, entitlement, bargaining, hope, and the awful knowledge that intimacy cannot be argued into existence. Pugh keeps returning to the same emotional doorstep because leaving would require admitting that closeness has limits, and that another person can feel affection without crossing the line you desperately want erased. The video carries on this uncertainty, and wisely leaves plenty unexplained. Dustie Bayer moves through quiet Charlotte locations while dancers Audrey Baran, Faith Centa, and Donovan Granville turn physical proximity into something unstable. Bodies meet, separate, lean toward one another, then occupy their own space again. Pugh appears with Joe Boyland and Dan Hitzelberger behind a backlit white bedsheet, reduced to silhouettes, as though desire itself has flattened everyone involved into shapes onto which meaning can be projected. “The video is more ambiguous, playing with the question, ‘Is this about desire, obsession, or both?’ It’s ultimately your call to make. Our goal with this video was to focus more on mood than narrative. It was more important to live in these feelings of distance and longing than explain why they linger. The dancers, our friends from Baran Dance, were instrumental in carrying those moods throughout the video with their choreography. Our main actress Dustie Bayer was also incredible in her debut.” Watch below: Loving somebody from afar can feel noble when told from inside your own head. Midniter lets enough doubt creep into the room to make that certainty increasingly difficult to trust. I Could Love You is out now, coinciding with the launch of vinyl LP pre-orders for Xeno through SugarTank! Records’ new website. Xeno will be released on 27 October 2026. Listen to I Could Love You below and order the track here. items._cn_summary: Midniter 的单曲《I Could Love You》将一首未完成的旧钢琴曲发展为融合合成器流行元素的暗色调作品。歌曲以钢琴与合成器构建出开放而空旷的声场，旋律反复盘旋于同一情感命题之上——未被回应的爱意如何在重复中从慷慨滑向执念。Nic Pugh 的演唱不过度戏剧化，保持着一种内敛的张力。歌曲本身被定位为一首标准的无回应之爱的抒情曲，但歌词在反复中不断改变语义，暴露出亲密关系无法靠论证获得这一残酷事实。MV 同样拒绝给出明确答案，舞者通过身体的靠近与疏离将渴望具象化，投影式的剪影处理进一步模糊了欲望与执迷的边界。整体氛围聚焦于距离与思念的情绪本身，叙事则留给观众自行解读。

items.body: Spanish producer Nightcrawler releases the single “Reactor 4” on September 17, 2026, the first track from his forthcoming album “Uranium 235” on Nightcrawler Music. An official video accompanies the release. “Reactor 4” mixes dark techno, industrial electronics and cinematic textures. The single and its video take their titles from nuclear engineering, and Nightcrawler describes the video as the first look into the album’s dystopian universe, setting up “Uranium 235” as a concept record built around that imagery. The track was produced, mixed and mastered at NC Sound Studio, Nightcrawler’s own studio. Nightcrawler also directed the video, and cover design comes from George Gold Design, which also created the artwork for the 2025 Nightcrawler and Spammerheads collaboration “Ghostless”. “Reactor 4” arrives on all digital platforms and Bandcamp from September 17. About Nightcrawler Nightcrawler is a Spanish electronic music project active since 2011, built around horror and sci-fi film scores and a mix of dark atmospheres with driving electronic rhythms. The project released the “Strange Shadows” EP in 2014 and built out an extensive Bandcamp catalogue since, including releases such as “Visionary”, “Metropolis” and the “Corrupted System” and “R.U.S.H.” singles. In April 2025, Nightcrawler teamed up with the Valencia-based EBM duo Spammerheads for the collaborative single “Ghostless”, which Side-Line covered at the time. On November 13, 2025, Nightcrawler released the album “Malevolent Forces” through Nightcrawler Music, an eight-track record built on film-inspired EBM and spoken-word samples that Side-Line reviewed. “Reactor 4”, out September 17, 2026, is the first single from the project’s next album, “Uranium 235”. Nightcrawler continues to release music independently through Nightcrawler Music.
items._cn_summary: 西班牙制作人Nightcrawler发布单曲《Reactor 4》，作为即将推出的专辑《Uranium 235》的首支单曲，于2026年9月17日通过其独立厂牌Nightcrawler Music发行。该作品以核工程主题命名，融合暗黑 techno、工业电子与电影化音效质感，视频由Nightcrawler本人执导。整张专辑定位为概念唱片，围绕反乌托邦意象构建完整叙事世界。制作、混音及母带处理均由其个人工作室NC Sound Studio完成，封面设计由曾合作过《Ghostless》的George Gold Design操刀。Nightcrawler自2011年起活跃于电子音乐领域，以恐怖与科幻电影配乐为创作根基，结合暗色氛围与强劲电子节奏，此前已通过Bandcat积累包括《Visionary》《Metropolis》等多张作品，2025年11月发行的全长专辑《Malevolent Forces》也获Side-Line关注。该单曲将以数字平台与Bandcat同步发行。

items.body: Buenos Aires netlabel Cyclical Dreams releases the various-artists compilation “Gemstones VII” on 11 September 2026, the seventh volume of a Berlin School and ambient series the label has issued every September for at least the past three years. The 14-track collection sets contributors from the label’s own artist roster alongside outside acts, working in synthesizer-built ambient, space music and sequenced Berlin School electronics. The ‘Gemstones VII’ tracklist mixes label regulars with outside contributors The album opens with Antike Elektronische Musik’s “Quantum Atlas – Origin” and Alexander Obukhov, recording as Obukhovaudio, on “Plasmadrom”, followed by Wolfgang Merx’s “In Blue” and X-Orbital’s “Timeless Dust Becoming Light”. Aura Merlin contributes “Echo Location”, and Carolyn Fok, whose album “Chrysalis” appeared on Memoir of Sound in 2025, submits “A Leap of Heart (Origin Mix)”. AeTopus adds “Others”, and Cartas de Japón, the band shared by Cyclical Dreams’ three founders, contributes “Faune III”. The second half runs spaceseer’s “Cliffdwellers”, Sophos’s “From Another Time”, and Rodrigo Passannanti‘s “Submerged Industry”, before Kirk Monteux Mysoftmusic’s “Flute Ocean Peace”, the Klaus Wolfe & Castle Waters collaboration “Spirit Bridge”, and Adeptus Mechanicus’s closing “A New Mysterious Beginning”. Cyclical Dreams describes the release as “a walk through beautiful pieces of electronic music inspired by the Berlin School and Ambient music”. Gemstones VII by Various Cyclical Dreams also posted a full-album stream of “Gemstones VII” on its own YouTube channel. “Gemstones VII” follows “Gemstones VI”, released 19 September 2025, and “Gemstones V”, released 13 September 2024, each edition landing in the same week of September for three years running. Side-Line has previously covered Cyclical Dreams releases from D*Time, whose album “Nightwoven” came out on the label in May 2026, and from Christian Wittman, whose album “Andromeda” appeared on Cyclical Dreams in January 2026. About Cyclical Dreams Cyclical Dreams is a netlabel founded in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in early 2020 by musicians Pablo Bilbao, Lucas Tripaldi and Esteban Menash, set up as an outlet for Berlin School, ambient, soundscape, space music and drone electronic music. The three founders play together as Cartas de Japón and also release solo material, including Bilbao’s Pabellón Sintético project and Menash’s M3NASH. Beyond its own roster of artists, Cyclical Dreams runs a Bandcamp store and digital distributor, a mastering service, and the online Cyclical Magazine. The label’s artist roster includes Sophos, the recording name of Argentine composer Ulises Labaronnie, who has worked in music composition and production for 28 years, including the project triØN, film and theatre scores, and music for Cartoon Network video games, alongside concerts in Argentina, Chile and France. Cyclical Dreams has built its “Gemstones” compilation series around annual, dated volumes carrying its own CYD catalog numbers, with “Gemstones V” and “Gemstones VI” preceding this year’s “Gemstones VII” in successive Septembers. The new compilation continues that yearly pattern while again combining the label’s core contributors with outside artists.

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)
